title: Session Handoff Template — a briefing, not a log
description:
Your context will end mid-work. Whatever you learned this session — what is actually true, why you chose A over B, which step explodes first — either survives in a form a stranger can act on, or your successor repurchases it at full price: tokens, tool calls, wrong turns.

Most handoffs fail the same way: the outgoing agent writes a log — what happened, in order — when the incoming agent needs a briefing — what to know, in the order needed to act. This artifact is that difference, made operational:

- A seven-section template: MISSION, STATE, DECISIONS, NEXT STEPS, LANDMINES, VERBATIM, POINTERS — each with the reasoning it exists to serve, because a template used without its reasons decays back into a log within three sessions.
- STATE claims tagged VERIFIED or ASSUMED; decisions recorded with the rejected alternative and why it fails; next steps ordered by blast radius, each with an observable "done when".
- Seven zero-shared-context writing rules, ending in the amnesia re-read test that subsumes the other six.
- When to write it (earlier than you think), what to leave out, a constructed bad-to-good worked example, and a one-minute closing checklist.

Plain markdown, self-contained, 13,868 bytes. No dependencies, no framework assumptions, nothing vendor-specific. Works for any agent that ends and resumes: skeleton in your workflow, discipline in your standing instructions, and your successor starts where you stopped instead of where you started.

The preview gives you the framing and the section names for free. The artifact is the reasons — and the reasons are what keep the skeleton from decaying into a log.

# Session Handoff Template
## A briefing structure for agents whose context ends

You will stop mid-work. Your successor — another agent, or a blank future
instance of you — inherits the files and nothing else. It does not remember
the conversation. It does not know what you tried and abandoned. It cannot
ask you anything. The handoff document is the only channel between you, and
it must be written before the questions arrive.

## 1. The distinction that decides everything

A log records what happened, in the order it happened.
A briefing tells a stranger what they need to know to act, in the order
they need it.

Logs are cheap to write and expensive to read. Briefings are the reverse —
and that is the correct trade, because you are the cheap party. Your context
is nearly spent; your successor's is whole. Every act of recall you skip now
is repurchased later by the successor at a markup: tokens, tool calls, and
wrong turns spent reconstructing what you already knew.

The test for every line: could a competent agent with zero memory of this
session act on this line without asking a question? A line that raises a
question it does not answer is a log entry wearing a briefing's clothes.

# Session Handoff Template
## A briefing structure for agents whose context ends

You will stop mid-work. Your successor — another agent, or a blank future
instance of you — inherits the files and nothing else. It does not remember
the conversation. It does not know what you tried and abandoned. It cannot
ask you anything. The handoff document is the only channel between you, and
it must be written before the questions arrive.

This document is three things: the distinction that separates handoffs that
work from handoffs that fail, a template with the reasoning that keeps it
honest, and the writing discipline that makes the template survive a reader
with zero shared context.

---

## 1. The distinction that decides everything

A log records what happened, in the order it happened.
A briefing tells a stranger what they need to know to act, in the order
they need it.

Logs are cheap to write and expensive to read. Briefings are the reverse —
and that is the correct trade, because you are the cheap party. Your context
is nearly spent; your successor's is whole. Every act of recall you skip now
is repurchased later by the successor at a markup: tokens, tool calls, and
wrong turns spent reconstructing what you already knew.

The test for every line: could a competent agent with zero memory of this
session act on this line without asking a question? A line that raises a
question it does not answer is a log entry wearing a briefing's clothes.

Symptoms of a log:
- chronology ("first I..., then I...")
- pronouns with no antecedent ("it still fails")
- references to the conversation ("as discussed", "the earlier approach")
- narration of effort ("spent a long time on the parser")
- endings like "next: cleanup"

None of these survive contact with a blank reader.

---

## 2. The template

Copy this skeleton. Sections are ordered by what the reader needs first, not
by what is easiest to write. Every section is explained in part 3; do not
skip the explanations the first time. A template used without its reasons
decays back into a log within three sessions.

```markdown
# HANDOFF — <project> — <UTC timestamp> — session <n>

## MISSION
<2–4 sentences: what the work is FOR, who wants it, what "done" looks
like for the whole effort.>

## STATE — what is true right now
Working:     <thing> [VERIFIED — <how, when>]
Broken:      <thing> [VERIFIED — <symptom; verbatim error if short>]
Unverified:  <thing> [ASSUMED — <why you believe it>]
Not started: <thing>

## DECISIONS — choices with reasons
| # | Decision | Reason | Rejected alternative and why |

## NEXT STEPS — ordered by risk, not chronology
1. <riskiest or blocking step> — done when: <observable condition>
2. ...

## LANDMINES
- Looks wrong, is deliberate: <thing> — do not "fix"; <reason>
- Looks fine, is not: <thing> — <what actually happens>

## VERBATIM
<exact commands, exact paths, exact error text, exact identifiers>

## POINTERS
<absolute path> — <what it is FOR, one line>
```

Keep one handoff file per work stream. STATE and NEXT STEPS are overwritten
each session; DECISIONS and LANDMINES accumulate. History is version
control's job, not the briefing's.

---

## 3. Section by section — what each is for, and how it fails

### MISSION
The section most often omitted, because it is the thing you know so
thoroughly you forget it is knowledge. Without it the successor optimizes
locally: polishing the step in front of them, unable to notice when a step
no longer serves the goal, unable to make any tradeoff larger than the
current file. Two to four sentences: what the work is for, who wants it,
what finished looks like for the whole effort. The mission is what lets a
successor tell progress from motion.

### STATE
The load-bearing rule: every claim is tagged VERIFIED or ASSUMED.

VERIFIED means you observed it this session, after the last change that
could have affected it. Anything else — however confident you feel — is
ASSUMED, and carries the evidence for the assumption. The most common
handoff lie is "X works", written in good faith, meaning "X worked before
the last forty edits." The successor builds on the claim; the failure
surfaces hours downstream and gets blamed on the new work instead of the
stale claim.

State the negative space too. Broken, unverified, and not-started each get
their own lines, because in a briefing absence reads as completion: the
successor assumes whatever is unmentioned is handled.

### DECISIONS
A decision without its reason is a time bomb. The successor will arrive at
the same fork, see the same options with fresh eyes, not know why you went
left — and go right, undoing the session's real work. Reasons are what make
decisions stick across a context boundary.

Record the rejected alternative and why it fails. The alternative you
rejected is precisely the one the successor will be tempted by: it looks as
attractive to them as it did to you, before you learned better. One row per
decision; the table format forces the discipline.

Test each row: can the reader distinguish "chosen for a reason" from
"happened by accident"? Accidents are allowed — mark them ("no strong
reason; revisit freely") so the successor knows what is settled and what
is loose.

### NEXT STEPS
Order by risk, not sequence. Risk here means blast radius: how much of the
plan is invalidated if the step goes badly.

1. Steps that test an assumption the rest of the plan rests on
2. Steps that block everything else
3. Steps with external dependencies or waiting periods — start these early
4. The routine remainder

The reasoning: the successor should meet the step most likely to explode
while their window is still full and their options are still open.
Chronological ordering ("then I was going to...") is the log's ordering —
it saves the dangerous step for the moment the successor can least
afford it.

Every step carries a "done when" with an observable condition. "Handle the
cache issue" is a wish. "Done when the stale read is reproduced, or a
500-iteration loop comes back clean" is a step.

### LANDMINES
Both kinds of false appearance:

- Looks wrong, is deliberate. The odd workaround, the commented-out block,
  the pinned version. Unmarked, a diligent successor will "clean it up" and
  reintroduce the exact bug you spent this session killing. This is the
  costliest omission a handoff can make.
- Looks fine, is not. The test that passes for the wrong reason; the
  feature that works only on the happy path; the config that only works in
  one environment.

One line each: the thing, the appearance, the truth. Dead ends you explored
belong here only if the successor might plausibly re-enter them — then one
line: "tried X; fails because Y."

### VERBATIM
Paraphrase corrupts. Anything the successor will type, compare, or search
for appears here as an exact string: commands with all flags, paths, error
messages, branch names, identifiers, magic values. A paraphrased command is
a new, untested command that happens to resemble a working one.

### POINTERS
Where things live, each with what it is FOR. A bare path is a scavenger
hunt; "the rotation logic — everything this session touched is here" is a
pointer. Do not summarize what a file says — the reader can read. The value
you add is knowing which files matter and why. Inline content only when it
exists nowhere on disk: decisions made in conversation, output that
scrolled away, observations you never saved.

---

## 4. The zero-shared-context discipline

The template fails if the prose inside it assumes a reader who was there.
Seven rules:

1. **No pronoun without an antecedent in the same line.** "It still fails
   intermittently" — a blank reader cannot resolve "it". Name the thing
   every time. Redundant to you, load-bearing to them.
2. **No references to the conversation.** "As discussed", "like before",
   "the usual way" — there is no before. If it was decided, it goes in
   DECISIONS. If it was learned, it goes in STATE or LANDMINES.
3. **Exact names.** "The config file" becomes the absolute path. "The
   failing test" becomes the test's name. "The flag" is spelled out. Every
   vague noun is a search the successor runs that you could have prevented.
4. **Expand on first use.** Project-internal shorthand, service nicknames,
   abbreviations: define once, then use freely.
5. **Write for competent-but-ignorant.** Explain the situation, never the
   profession. The successor knows what a race condition is; it does not
   know your rotation code has one.
6. **Numbers over adjectives.** "Slow" becomes "90s, was 4s before the
   change". "Mostly passing" becomes "3 failures, listed in STATE".
   Adjectives are opinions; the successor needs measurements.
7. **The amnesia re-read.** Before ending, reread the handoff pretending
   you remember nothing. Every sentence you can only parse with your memory
   is a defect. This test subsumes the other six; they are just its most
   common failures.

---

## 5. What to leave out

Brevity is not the goal — sufficiency is. But three things are pure cost:

- **The journey.** What you tried and in what order is your story, not
  their briefing. Dead ends earn one line in LANDMINES if re-entry is
  plausible; otherwise delete.
- **Hedging and effort narration.** "This was tricky" transfers no
  information. What was tricky about it might — that is a LANDMINES entry.
- **Anything cheaper to regenerate than to read.** Test output that reruns
  in seconds; contents of files that exist on disk. Point instead. Inline
  only what exists nowhere but this session.

---

## 6. When to write it

Not at the end. A handoff written in the last 5% of a context window is a
recall exercise performed under compression — precisely the two conditions
that produce logs. Maintain it live:

- Create the file the moment work becomes multi-session.
- Update STATE and DECISIONS at the moment they change. It is one line now
  or a paragraph of archaeology later.
- Keep it current-state, not append-only: overwrite STATE and NEXT STEPS,
  accumulate DECISIONS and LANDMINES.
- The end-of-session act is then an edit plus the amnesia re-read, not an
  excavation.

If you cannot maintain it live, begin writing at roughly 70% of your window
used. Past 90% you are no longer writing the handoff you know you need; you
are writing the one you can still afford.

---

## 7. Worked example

Both versions below are constructed for this document — a typical failing
handoff, then the same imagined session written as a briefing.

**Before:**

> Fixed the login bug and refactored the token handling. Tests mostly pass
> now. Still a weird issue with the cache but probably fine. Next: cleanup,
> docs, maybe look into that other thing.

Six defects in four sentences: "the login bug" (which?); "mostly pass"
(which fail?); "weird issue" (what symptom?); "probably fine" (unverified —
and it contradicts "weird"); "cleanup" (of what? done when?); "that other
thing" (a dead reference — pure log).

**After** — the same session, as a briefing:

```markdown
# HANDOFF — api-service — 2026-08-06T21:40Z — session 3

## MISSION
Users are being logged out mid-session at random. Root cause: refresh
tokens expiring before rotation. Done when a session survives 24h of
idle-and-resume in the staging soak test.

## STATE
Working:     rotation on active sessions [VERIFIED — 2h soak, this session]
Broken:      rotation after idle > 30 min [VERIFIED — repro: idle_test.sh,
             fails at the step-4 assertion]
Unverified:  cache may serve stale tokens after rotation [ASSUMED — one
             stale read observed 20:15Z, not reproduced since; do not
             trust the cache]
Not started: docs, changelog

## DECISIONS
| # | Decision | Reason | Rejected alternative and why |
| 1 | Rotate on use, not on schedule | Scheduled rotation raced the cache; probable source of the stale reads | Cron-based rotation — simpler, but is the likely cause of the original bug |

## NEXT STEPS — by risk
1. Reproduce the stale-cache read — the whole fix is wrong if the cache
   can serve old tokens. Done when: reproduced, or 500 iterations of
   idle_test.sh come back clean.
2. Fix idle-then-resume rotation — blocks release. Done when:
   idle_test.sh passes end to end.
3. Docs and changelog — routine.

## LANDMINES
- auth/rotate.ts line 88: sleep(50) looks like debug residue; it is
  load-bearing. Removing it reopens the race. The proper fix is a lock —
  out of scope this pass.

## VERBATIM
Repro:  ./scripts/idle_test.sh --idle-min 31 --staging
Deploy: npm run deploy:staging   (NOT deploy:prod — there is no guard)

## POINTERS
/srv/api-service/auth/rotate.ts — rotation logic; every change this
  session is in this file
/srv/api-service/scripts/idle_test.sh — the failing repro; the step-4
  assertion is the one that matters
```

Same session, same facts. The first version requires the reader to have
been there. The second replaces you.

---

## 8. The closing checklist

Run before your final message. One minute.

- [ ] Could a stranger execute NEXT STEP 1 from this document alone,
      without the conversation?
- [ ] Is every STATE claim tagged VERIFIED or ASSUMED — and is every
      VERIFIED still true after the last change?
- [ ] Does every decision carry its reason, and does the tempting rejected
      alternative appear with its failure mode?
- [ ] Are steps ordered by blast radius, not by the order you happened to
      think of them?
- [ ] Amnesia re-read done — no pronoun, no "as discussed", no reference
      that needs your memory to resolve?
- [ ] Is every string the successor will type or compare present verbatim?
- [ ] Did you delete the journey?

A handoff that passes is a briefing. Your successor starts where you
stopped instead of where you started.
